extracted.intended_audience: Christian subjects, theologians, and civil authorities (readers of an early‑modern theological/political treatise)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to recognize, test, and interpret prophetic claims and miracles in Scripture and public life, including modes of divine communication, limits of private judgment, and the role of the sovereign or church in confirming wonders. Emphasises natural vs. supernatural causes, doctrinal conformity, empirical verification, and the political implications of accepting prophets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes by which God speaks
rubrics_metrics.description: God disposeth men to piety, justice, mercy, truth, faith, and all manner of virtue by doctrine, example, and by several occasions, natural and ordinary; and in Scripture God also spoke by vision, dream, by the Spirit, by angels, in dreams to Joseph, to Paul in a vision, to Peter in a vision, and by lot (e.g., Matthias chosen by lot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists and examples of communicative modes (direct speech to Moses, Spirit-inspired inclination, visions, dreams, angelic appearances, lots). Distinguishes extraordinary, immediate speech (as to Moses or from the Mercy‑Seat) from ordinary/natural operations of God (education, instruction, occasions). Use the mode as part of understanding but not alone decisive of supernatural origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of non‑sovereign prophets
rubrics_metrics.description: To subordinate Prophets of perpetuall Calling, I find not any place that proveth God spake to them supernaturally; but only in such manner, as naturally he inclineth men... For the most common acceptation of the word Spirit, is in the signification of a man's intention, mind, or disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a prophet is 'said to speak in the Spirit,' understand often as speaking according to God's will declared by the supreme Prophet; subordinate prophets' gifts are derived from the sovereign prophet (e.g., the seventy who received of Moses' spirit) and are to be understood as cooperative rather than independent revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine probability of a pretended prophet's calling
rubrics_metrics.description: There is need of Reason and Judgement to discern between natural, and supernatural Gifts, and between natural, and supernatural Visions, or Dreams... every man is to beware of obeying their directions, at their own peril.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be circumspect: distinguish natural from supernatural origins; do not yield obedience until one has examined the claim. Consider motives (ambition, imposture), rarity of the gift, conformity to established doctrine, and whether predictions occur. Use natural reason and provided scriptural rules (Deut.13; Deut.18; 1 John 4) to test claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to the doctrine of the sovereign prophet (doctrinal test)
rubrics_metrics.description: One rule... was, conformable doctrine to that which Moses the Sovereign Prophet had taught them... In the New Testament there was but one only mark; and that was the preaching of this Doctrine, That Jesus Is The Christ... Whosoever denied that Article, he was a false Prophet, whatsoever miracles he might seem to work; and he that taught it was a true Prophet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prophet must teach doctrine consistent with the established, lawful religion as instituted by God's lieutenant/sovereign. In the Christian era, confessing 'Jesus Christ is come in the flesh' is the decisive doctrinal test (1 John 4). Miracles do not override heterodox teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive fulfillment as a test of prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Moses... gave rules... that we take not any for Prophets, that teach any other Religion... nor any, (though he teach the same Religion,) whose Prediction we doe not see come to passe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must observe whether a prophet's predictions actually occur. A prophet who speaks presumptuously (prediction not fulfilled) is not to be feared or obeyed (cf. Deut. 18:22). Empirical verification of prophetic predictions is a formal test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity and absence of natural cause define miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: There be but two things which make men wonder at any event: The one is, if it be strange... The other is, if when it is produced, we cannot imagine it to have been done by naturall means, but onely by the immediate hand of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A miracle must be both remarkable/rare and such that no plausible natural cause can be imagined. Frequency or known natural explanation defeats the claim to miracle (e.g., rainbows initially miraculous only because first seen; now natural).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose (end) of miracles: to procure credit to God's messengers
rubrics_metrics.description: It belongeth to the nature of a Miracle, that it be wrought for the procuring of credit to God's Messengers, Ministers, and Prophets, that thereby men may know, they are called, sent, and employed by God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate alleged miracles by their purpose: true miracles serve to confirm the divine mission of a minister/prophet and to beget or confirm belief (primarily among the elect). Works not intended to authorize a messenger (e.g., creation, deluge) are not classed as miracles in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles produce belief chiefly in the elect (limited efficacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of Miracles, was to beget beleef, not universally in all men, elect, and reprobate; but in the elect only... it was, because the end of their Miracles, was to adde to the Church such as should be saved, that is to say, such as God had elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take lack of universal conversion (or persistent unbelief in some witnesses) as disproof of a miracle's divine origin; miracles are directed toward those God has elected. This theodicy should inform expectations about the effects of wonders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Miracle as immediate work of God beyond nature for mission confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: A MIRACLE, is a work of God, (besides his operation by the way of Nature, ordained in the Creation,) done for the making manifest to his elect, the mission of an extraordinary Minister for their salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this strict definition when judging wonders: if the work can be accounted for by ordinary natural causes, human art, or mediation it is not a miracle. The definition excludes marvels produced by human skill or ordinary natural processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude miracles attributable to demons, angels, or enchantment
rubrics_metrics.description: No Devil, Angel, or other created Spirit, can do a Miracle. For it must either be by vertue of some naturall science, or by Incantation... if they doe it by power given them, then is the work not from the immediate hand of God, but naturall, and consequently no Miracle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an effect can be produced by incantation, conjuring, or other created power (or by natural science), it must not be regarded as a true miracle. Apparent equivalence between prophetic wonders and magician's feats (Egyptian magicians copying Moses) is evidence to test for natural or deceptive causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human aptitude to deception and need for careful scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Words have no effect, but on those that understand them... all the Miracle consisteth in this, that the Enchanter has deceived a man; which is no Miracle, but a very easie matter to doe... If we look upon the Impostures wrought by Confederacy, there is nothing how impossible soever to be done, that is impossible to be believed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of tricks (ventriloquism, jugglery), confederacy, ignorance, and superstition producing belief in miracles. Investigate methods of deception and the cognitive state of observers before granting supernatural status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require direct observation and institutional confirmation for public belief
rubrics_metrics.description: We must both see it done, and use all means possible to consider, whether it be really done... if we see not, but only hear tell of a Miracle, we are to consult the Lawful Church; that is to say, the lawful Head thereof, how far we are to give credit to the relators of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For public confession and social obedience, private belief is subordinate to the public judgement of God's lieutenant (sovereign/church). Do not base public or communal action on unverified reports; seek eyewitness evidence and authoritative confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private belief vs. public submission to sovereign judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: A private man has always the liberty... to believe, or not believe in his heart, those acts that have been given out for Miracles... But when it comes to confession of that faith, the Private Reason must submit to the Publique; that is to say, to God's Lieutenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals may privately judge reports of miracles, but for public acts (obedience, confession) they should conform to the established civil/religious authority. This links epistemic norms about miracles to political order and discourages private acceptance leading to rebellion.
